title: MOSFET layout, cross section, CMOS and symbols

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A MOSFET is a MOS capacitor with two extra terminals. Starting from the p-type body, gate oxide and n+ polysilicon gate you already know, add two heavily doped **n+** regions at either end of the gate: the **source** and the **drain**. When the gate inverts the surface, the electron layer connects them and current flows.

The geometry that matters is the channel **length** \(L\), from source to drain, and the **width** \(W\), across. Current scales with \(W/L\). The device is symmetric; the source is simply the n+ end at the lower potential. The body is tied to the lowest supply so the source and drain junctions stay reverse biased. **CMOS** puts both types on one chip: NMOS directly in the p substrate, and PMOS (p+ source and drain) inside an n-well. In the symbols, the PMOS has a bubble on its gate, because it turns on when the gate goes low.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Gate oxide capacitance per area and total:
\[ C_{ox} = \frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}}, \qquad C_G \approx C_{ox}WL \]
Unit help: \(1\ \mathrm{F/cm^2} = 10^7\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).
Drain current \(\propto \dfrac{W}{L}\) at a fixed bias.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A process has \(t_{ox} = 6\ \mathrm{nm}\):
\[ C_{ox} = \frac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}} \approx 5.75\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2} \]
A transistor with \(W = 4\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) and \(L = 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) has \(C_G \approx 5.75 \times 1.0 \approx 5.75\ \mathrm{fF}\) and \(W/L = 16\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Swapping \(W\) and \(L\). \(L\) is along the current.
- Assuming source and drain differ physically; the voltages decide.
- Forgetting the PMOS needs an n-type body (the n-well).
- Leaving the body floating, which can forward-bias a source or drain junction.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Next you will find out when the channel exists and how its current depends on \(V_{GS}\) and \(V_{DS}\), leading to the regions of operation and the square law.
